title: The Nervous System and Sense Organs

blocks.text: You step on a nail in a dusty compound and your foot is already off the ground before you have had time to shout. No conscious plan was needed: a message raced from the skin to the spinal cord and back to the leg muscles in a fraction of a second. That pathway is a reflex arc, built from neurones — and the same kind of cell lets you see a approaching danfo and hear its horn.

blocks.markdown:
## The neurone and the nervous system

A **neurone** is a nerve cell specialised to carry electrical impulses.

- **Dendrites** receive impulses and pass them towards the cell body.
- The **cell body** contains the nucleus and most of the cytoplasm.
- The **axon** is a long fibre that carries the impulse away from the cell body.
- A fatty **myelin sheath** (made by Schwann cells) insulates the axon and speeds conduction; gaps in it are the nodes of Ranvier.
- At the end, **synaptic knobs** release a chemical transmitter across a **synapse** — the tiny gap between one neurone and the next.

The **central nervous system (CNS)** is the brain and spinal cord. The **peripheral nervous system (PNS)** is all the cranial and spinal nerves that connect the CNS to the rest of the body.

**Sensory (afferent) neurones** carry impulses from receptors to the CNS. **Motor (efferent) neurones** carry impulses from the CNS to effectors (muscles or glands). **Relay neurones** (interneurones) lie entirely in the CNS and link sensory to motor neurones.

blocks.title: Synapse
blocks.text: The microscopic gap between the axon terminal of one neurone and the dendrite or cell body of the next. The impulse cannot jump the gap as electricity; a transmitter substance is released, diffuses across, and starts a new impulse in the following neurone. Synapses ensure impulses travel in one direction only.

rows: Receptor (e.g. pain ending in the skin)
Detects the stimulus and starts an impulse
Carries the impulse into the spinal cord through the dorsal root
Passes the impulse to a relay neurone, then to a motor neurone
Carries the impulse out through the ventral root to the effector
Responds — the muscle contracts or the gland secretes
blocks.caption: The reflex arc — learn this sequence in order

blocks.markdown:
## The eye and the ear

**Eye.** Light is bent (refracted) first by the transparent **cornea**, then by the **lens**. The **iris** is a coloured muscular ring that changes the size of the **pupil** to control how much light enters. The **retina** contains **rods** (dim light, black and white) and **cones** (bright light, colour, concentrated at the fovea). Impulses leave in the **optic nerve**; the blind spot has no receptors. **Accommodation** is the change in lens shape for near and distant objects: for a near object the ciliary muscles contract, the suspensory ligaments slacken and the lens becomes fatter; for a distant object the opposite occurs and the lens thins.

**Ear.** The **pinna** collects sound. The **tympanum** (eardrum) vibrates. Three **ossicles** — malleus, incus and stapes — amplify the vibration and pass it to the oval window. The **cochlea** contains the organ of Corti, which converts vibration into impulses for hearing. The **semicircular canals** detect rotation of the head and so serve balance. The Eustachian tube equalises pressure on the two sides of the tympanum.

items: A reflex is rapid, automatic and often protective; the brain is informed but does not have to decide before the response happens.
The cell body of a sensory neurone lies in the dorsal-root ganglion; the cell body of a motor neurone lies in the grey matter of the spinal cord.
Short sight (myopia) is corrected with a concave lens; long sight (hypermetropia) with a convex lens.
Damage to the cochlea affects hearing; damage to the semicircular canals affects balance — examiners use this distinction constantly.

blocks.title: Tracing a reflex from a hot pot
blocks.prompt: A cook in a buka touches a hot pot and immediately pulls the hand away. Trace the pathway of this reflex, naming each neurone and the location of the synapses, and state why the response can occur before pain is consciously felt.

steps.text: Heat (the stimulus) is detected by temperature/pain receptors in the skin of the fingers.
A sensory neurone carries the impulse through the dorsal root into the grey matter of the spinal cord.
At synapses in the spinal cord the impulse is passed to a relay neurone and then to a motor neurone.
The motor neurone leaves through the ventral root and stimulates the effector — the biceps and related muscles — which contract and withdraw the hand.
A branch of the pathway also informs the brain, so pain is felt a moment later. The withdrawal itself does not wait for the brain, which is why the reflex is faster than a considered action.

blocks.answer: Receptor → sensory neurone (dorsal root) → synapse and relay in the spinal cord → motor neurone (ventral root) → muscle. The brain is informed afterwards, so the hand moves before pain is consciously registered.

blocks.title: WAEC and JAMB tip
blocks.text: For accommodation, remember: near = ciliary muscles contract = ligaments slacken = lens fat. Distant = ciliary muscles relax = ligaments taut = lens thin. Mixing those four statements is the most expensive error on this topic. In the ear, cochlea = hearing and semicircular canals = balance; do not swap them.

points: A neurone has dendrites, a cell body, an axon (often myelinated) and synaptic knobs; a synapse uses a chemical transmitter and is one-way.
The CNS is brain plus spinal cord; the PNS is the nerves; neurones are sensory, relay or motor.
A reflex arc is receptor → sensory neurone → spinal cord synapses (relay) → motor neurone → effector.
The cornea and lens refract light; the iris controls the pupil; rods and cones in the retina detect light; the optic nerve carries impulses.
The pinna, tympanum and ossicles transmit sound to the cochlea (hearing); semicircular canals detect balance.
